title: Variable Thresholds for Phosphorylation Targets of the ERK Signaling Pathway
projectDescription: Cell fates regulated by ERK/MAP kinases respond to different thresholds of signaling strength.  In mammalian cells, conditions that activate ERK to submaximal levels are sufficient to sustain proliferation, survival and transformation, while stimuli that activate ERK to very high levels often lead to cell death or cell cycle arrest. But while this “Goldilocks effect” is well known, the mechanisms have never been fully explained. In particular, threshold responses have been shown at the level of transcription and cell state changes, but whether phosphorylation responses upstream of these events also respond to thresholds is unknown. Here we used mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics to ask if molecular events in the ERK pathway respond to different thresholds of signaling strength, by quantifying changes in phosphorylation of pathway targets against the occupancy of the two activating phosphosites in ERK. The results show that most phosphorylation events track ERK activation faithfully, responding linearly with increasing 2P-ERK occupancy. But some sites respond nonlinearly, reaching maximal phosphorylation when 2P-ERK exceeds lower thresholds (10-40%), or increasing substantially after 2P-ERK exceeds higher thresholds (>60%). Low threshold sites are found on transcriptional repressors that facilitate proliferation when inactivated by ERK/RSK phosphorylation. By contrast, high threshold sites are found on proteins that are recruited to dsDNA breaks and mediate DNA repair. Measurement of phosphorylation occupancies also revealed unexpected differences between cell states not apparent from inhibitor fold-changes. Our findings demonstrate that signaling thresholds exist at the level of the phosphoproteome, providing potential mechanisms for regulating cellular responses to pathway strength.
sampleProcessingProtocol: WM239a cells stably transfected with empty vector were treated for 2 h with trametinib [final concentrations: 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100 nM (replicates 1-3)] or DMSO control. WM239a cells stably transfected with BRAF(V600E) were treated for 2 h with trametinib [final concentrations: 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300 nM (replicate 1); 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000 nM (replicates 2 and 3)] or DMSO control. Cells were harvested in lysis buffer [200 mM Hepes, pH 8.5, 5% (w/v) SDS, 10 mM TCEP, 40 mM chloroacetamide, 1X PhosStop (Roche)] and boiled at 95°C for 10 min. Total protein was quantified by Pierce 660nm protein assay (Pierce). Lysates were digested with trypsin/lys-C mix (Promega) at 37°C overnight with a protease:protein ratio of 1:100 (w/w) using the SP3 method. Samples were eluted from SP3 beads in Hepes, pH 8.5. Peptide concentration was quantified by tryptophan fluorescence. 200 µg of peptide were labeled with TMT tandem mass tags (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a 1:4 peptide:TMT ratio (w/w) for 2 hours at room temperature. Samples within each plex were pooled and cleaned up with an HLB Oasis 6cc (150mg) cartridge (Waters). 10% of each HLB elution was dried by vacuum centrifugation and saved for whole proteome analysis. The rest of the HLB elutions underwent TiO2 phosphopeptide enrichment. Approximately 20-30 µg of each whole proteome and phosphoproteome multiplexed sample were fractionated with offline high pH reversed-phase chromatography. All fractions were dried by vacuum centrifugation, and resuspended in 3% acetonitrile in 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw data dependent acquisition files were searched against the UniProt Homo sapiens databases UP000005640 using MaxQuant version 2.0.3.0 with Trypsin/P + LysC digestion with up to 2 missed cleavages. Cysteine carbamidomethylation, TMT-labeled lysine, and TMT-labeled peptide N-termini were set as fixed modifications. Methionine oxidation, protein N-terminal acetylation, and serine/threonine/tyrosine phosphorylation were searched as variable modifications. To check labeling efficiency, TMT-labeled lysine and TMT-labeled peptide N-termini were set as variable modifications in separate searches. All peptides and proteins were thresholded at a 1% false discovery rate (FDR), and reverse sequences and potential contaminants were removed. TMT reporter ion intensities were isotope-corrected using MaxQuant according to the manufacturer-provided batch-specific isotopic impurities of each TMT channel and normalized using CONSTANd constrained optimization. For peptide quantification, intensities were summed for the same modified peptide sequence.
